key_terms.meaning: Two-dimensional cutting in which the cutting edge is perpendicular to the cutting velocity, so forces appear in one plane and chip flow is normal to the edge.
Cutting in which the cutting edge is inclined at angle i to the normal of the cutting velocity, so the chip flows sideways along the face.
r = t₁ / t₂ = sin φ / cos(φ − α), where t₁ is uncut chip thickness, t₂ is chip thickness, φ is shear angle and α is rake angle.
Force circle that resolves the measured cutting force Fc and thrust force Ft into shear force, friction force and normal force on the rake face.
Angle for which tan β = μ = F / N, with F the friction force and N the normal force on the rake face.
Seven-number code (ASA system) giving back rake, side rake, end relief, side relief, end cutting edge angle, side cutting edge angle and nose radius.
Angle between the tool face and a line parallel to the tool shank, measured in the back rake plane; it slopes the face towards the shank.
Angle between the side cutting edge and the side of the tool shank; it spreads the cut and thins the chip at entry.
Radius in millimetres at the tool tip joining the side and end cutting edges; a larger radius gives better finish but more chatter.
Ability of a tool material to stay hard at the high temperature of the cutting zone; it decides the usable cutting speed.
Liquid or mist applied to the cutting zone to carry away heat, reduce friction and flush chips; water-soluble, straight oil or semi-synthetic.
Wear land measured on the relief face of the tool, in millimetres; the standard criterion is VB = 0.3 mm for a carbide tool.
Dish-shaped wear on the rake face caused by diffusion and adhesion at high temperature, common when cutting steel at high speed.
Welded layer of work material sticking on the tool nose at low speed; it breaks away and leaves a rough surface.
V Tⁿ = C, where V is cutting speed in m/min, T is tool life in min, C is a constant and n is about 0.1 for HSS and 0.2–0.3 for carbide.
Cutting speed of the material for a 60 min tool life divided by that of free-cutting steel, expressed as a percentage; higher means easier to cut.
Distance the tool advances per revolution of the work (turning, mm/rev) or per tooth (milling, mm/tooth).
Climb milling in which the cutter rotation and table feed are in the same direction, so the chip starts at maximum thickness.
Generating process using a rotating worm-shaped hob whose rotation is synchronized with the gear blank to cut all teeth in one pass.
Finishing process using bonded abrasive sticks, rotated and reciprocated inside a bore to correct shape and improve finish.

takeaways: Metal cutting is shear concentrated in a thin zone: the uncut layer becomes a chip only because it shears along the shear plane.
Orthogonal cutting is the clean two-dimensional model used for equations; real turning, milling and drilling are oblique.
The Merchant circle turns two measurable forces into the friction on the rake face and the shear force on the shear plane.
A single-point tool needs a fixed order of seven numbers so that any grinder can reproduce it from a drawing.
Tool material is chosen for hot hardness; the cutting temperature, not room-temperature hardness, sets the limit.
Tool life drops steeply as cutting speed rises, and Taylor's equation captures that fall in one line.
Lathe, drilling and milling are separated by their relative tool–work motion, not by the shape of the machine.
Gear teeth are made either by copying the space with a form cutter or by generating the involute through synchronized motion.
Abrasive finishing removes very little material with many hard grains, which is why it improves accuracy and finish but not size.
bank_note: Long questions in this unit almost always combine a labelled sketch with a derivation (Merchant's relations, Taylor's equation), a standard tool-signature list, and a comparison or numerical, so answer with the sketch, the formula with symbols defined, and the number with units.

bank.q: Define orthogonal and oblique cutting. With a neat sketch, explain how the chip forms, naming the deformation zones and the shear plane.
outline: Orthogonal: cutting edge perpendicular to cutting velocity, 2-D forces, chip flows normal to edge
Oblique: edge inclined at angle i, chip flows sideways, 3-D forces, longer tool life
Sketch with tool, chip, shear plane, rake angle α, shear angle φ
Three zones: primary shear zone, secondary (friction) zone at rake face, tertiary zone at flank
Uncut chip thickness t₁, chip thickness t₂, chip thickness ratio r

bank.q: Draw the Merchant circle diagram for orthogonal cutting and derive expressions for shear force, friction force and coefficient of friction in terms of Fc, Ft and rake angle α.
outline: Define Fc (cutting force) and Ft (thrust force) with units
Merchant circle construction with rake angle α, shear angle φ, friction angle β
Fs = Fc cos φ − Ft sin φ and Fn = Fc sin φ + Ft cos φ
F = Fc sin α + Ft cos α and N = Fc cos α − Ft sin α
μ = tan β = F / N
Shear plane area As = (t₁ b) / sin φ and shear stress τ = Fs / As

bank.q: Sketch a single-point turning tool and explain all seven elements of the ASA tool signature with a typical value for each.
outline: Label face, flank, end cutting edge, side cutting edge, nose, nose radius, shank
Order: back rake, side rake, end relief, side relief, ECEA, SCEA, nose radius
Example signature such as 0-7-6-8-15-16-0.8 mm
Meaning of positive and negative back rake, and effect of SCEA on chip thinning
Effect of nose radius on surface finish and chatter

bank.q: State the properties required of a cutting tool material and compare high speed steel, cemented carbide, coated carbide and ceramics.
outline: Hot hardness, wear resistance, toughness, low friction, thermal conductivity, cost
HSS: tough, cheap, usable up to about 600 °C, good for drills and taps
Carbide: high hot hardness, low toughness, speeds several times HSS
Coated carbide: TiN/TiC/Al₂O₃ layers reduce diffusion and crater wear
Ceramics and CBN: very high speed, poor shock resistance, used for hard and cast iron work
Selection table with speed range and application

bank.q: Explain flank wear, crater wear and built-up edge in a single-point tool, and state how each one affects tool life and surface finish.
outline: Flank wear VB on relief face, caused by abrasion, measured in mm, criterion 0.3 mm
Crater wear on rake face, caused by diffusion and adhesion at high temperature
Notch wear at depth-of-cut line, oxidation and work-hardening effect
BUE forms at low speed and high friction, breaks away leaving rough surface
Effect of each on dimensional accuracy, forces and vibration
Remedies: speed increase to avoid BUE, coatings, coolant

bank.q: In an orthogonal cutting test on mild steel, Fc = 900 N and Ft = 600 N at rake angle 10° and shear angle 25°. Calculate the shear force, friction force, normal force and coefficient of friction.
outline: Fs = Fc cos φ − Ft sin φ with φ = 25°
Fn = Fc sin φ + Ft cos φ
F = Fc sin α + Ft cos α with α = 10°
N = Fc cos α − Ft sin α
μ = F / N and friction angle β = tan⁻¹ μ
Correct units in newtons and a short comment on the value of μ

bank.q: A carbide tool lasts 60 min at a cutting speed of 40 m/min. Using Taylor's equation with n = 0.125, find the cutting speed for a tool life of 20 min and comment on the result.
outline: Write VTⁿ = C with symbols defined
Find C from 40 × 60^0.125
Solve V = C / 20^0.125
State the answer in m/min
Comment: speed rises but only modestly because n is small

bank.q: Calculate the machining time to turn a mild steel bar of 50 mm diameter and 200 mm length at a cutting speed of 30 m/min with a feed of 0.2 mm/rev in a single pass.
outline: N = 1000 V / (π D), state N in rpm
Machining time T = L / (f N)
Substitute L = 200 mm, f = 0.2 mm/rev
Answer in minutes
Note that approach and overtravel lengths add to L in practice

bank.q: Estimate the material removal rate and the drilling time for a 20 mm diameter hole through a 25 mm thick plate at a spindle speed of 400 rpm and a feed of 0.2 mm/rev.
outline: Cutting speed V = π D N / 1000
Feed rate = f × N in mm/min
Time = plate thickness plus approach / feed rate
MRR = (π/4) D² × feed rate, answer in mm³/min
Comment on effect of increasing feed on time and thrust force

bank.q: Select a tool material and a cutting fluid for high-speed turning of mild steel, and justify the selection using cutting temperature and wear arguments.
outline: Cutting temperature rises with speed; links to crater and flank wear
Coated carbide chosen for hot hardness and low diffusion wear
Water-soluble cutting fluid for cooling at high speed
Straight oil or EP additive for low-speed heavy cuts and tapping
Effect on built-up edge and surface finish
Cost and shop-floor constraints

bank.q: Merchant's shear angle relation predicts φ from α and β. Examine its assumptions and explain why measured shear angles often differ from the predicted value.
outline: State 2φ + β − α = 90° with symbols defined
Assumptions: sharp tool, continuous chip, uniform stress on shear plane, constant μ, no BUE, no strain hardening
Shear stress varies with normal stress on shear plane (Lee–Shaffer, modified Merchant)
Strain rate and temperature dependence of shear strength
Presence of BUE, tool wear and edge radius
Conclusion: good trend predictor, not an exact value

bank.q: A tool on a lathe fails well before its rated tool life. Analyze the possible wear mechanisms and cutting conditions responsible, and recommend remedies.
outline: Check speed, feed and depth of cut against Taylor life for the tool
Abrasion from hard inclusions or casting skin
Adhesion and BUE at low speed with poor fluid
Diffusion and crater wear at excessive speed
Chipping from interrupted cut, backlash, lack of rigidity
Notch wear from work-hardened surface at depth-of-cut line
Remedies: reduce speed, change grade or coating, rigid setup, correct coolant, grind tool

bank.q: Compare gear forming and gear generation. Evaluate which method suits a batch of 20,000 identical spur gears, giving reasons.
outline: Forming: form cutter shaped as tooth space, indexing between teeth, cutter specific to module and tooth number
Generation: hob or shaper cutter generating the involute; one cutter covers a range of tooth numbers
Accuracy and surface finish comparison
Time per gear and tool cost
For large batches hobbing wins on accuracy, rate and tool inventory
Mention gear shaping for shoulder and internal gears

bank.q: Analyze the causes of grinding burn and surface cracks, and evaluate the role of cutting fluid, wheel grade and depth of cut in controlling them.
outline: Heat generated by rubbing and ploughing of dull grains
Burn marks and temper colours, tensile residual stress, cracks
Wheel too hard or glazed, no self-sharpening
Excessive depth of cut and infeed rate
Fluid type, pressure and delivery method; neat oil versus water-soluble
Softer grade, coarser grit, open structure, wheel dressing
Speed selection and use of continuous dress creep grinding

glossary.def: Removing material as chips with a harder cutting tool to bring a part to shape, size and finish.
Two-dimensional cutting where the cutting edge is perpendicular to the cutting velocity.
Cutting where the cutting edge is inclined to the cutting velocity, so the chip flows at an angle.
The layer of work material that has been sheared off and slides over the rake face.
Narrow zone, treated as a plane at angle φ, where the uncut layer shears into a chip.
Angle between the tool face and the reference plane; positive rake cuts freely, negative rake strengthens the edge.
Angle between the flank of the tool and the machined surface, which stops the flank rubbing.
Top surface of the tool over which the chip slides.
Surface of the tool facing the newly machined work surface, below the cutting edge.
A force-circle construction that resolves measured cutting and thrust forces into shear and friction components.
Angle φ between the shear plane and the cutting velocity direction.
Angle β whose tangent equals the coefficient of friction at the chip–tool interface.
Welded lump of work material on the tool nose that forms at low speed and breaks off periodically.
Time, in minutes, for which a tool cuts before wear reaches the chosen criterion, usually VB = 0.3 mm.
How easily a material can be cut, judged by tool life, forces, power, surface finish and chip form.
Distance moved by the tool per revolution of the work or per tooth of the cutter.
Thickness of the layer removed in one pass, measured perpendicular to the machined surface.
Conventional milling where cutter rotation opposes the table feed, so the chip starts at zero thickness.
Equal rotation of the work between cuts, done on a dividing head, to space teeth or flutes.
Gear generating process in which a worm-shaped hob and the blank rotate in a fixed ratio.
Low-speed abrasive finishing of a bore with rotating and reciprocating bonded sticks.
Finishing with loose abrasive in a fluid between the work and a soft lap, giving very fine finish and flatness.
Finishing with a fine stone oscillated at small amplitude and light pressure to remove fragmented surface layers.
Volume of material cut per unit time, usually in mm³/min, equal to speed × feed × depth of cut in turning.
